t69d_st1g: The words you use in this kind of work direct attention. So when the painful or negative thing isn't itself what needs naming, it's better to use words that point toward what you want to strengthen, whether that's a relationship or something you want to be able to do. "Let's help you build more ways to feel cared for and supported" usually gives the mind a clearer direction than bringing up a label like "dependency" just to deny it or argue with it (your mind hears "dependency" either way). With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make the direction easy to imagine: warmth, protection, choice, steadiness, connection, honesty, courage, rest, or whatever is really needed.
t69d_st1h: Partway through a session you might catch yourself saying "I'm not dependent, I'm not dependent." Guess what your mind just heard? So unless the painful thing really is what needs naming, talk toward what you want to strengthen, a relationship or something you'd like to be able to do. "Let's help you build more ways to feel cared for and supported" gives it somewhere to go. With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make that easy to imagine, warmth or rest, whatever's really needed.
t69d_st2m: Grief is grief, though. Partway through all that steering, you might think, "But it really was dangerous," and if it was, it should be called dangerous. Same goes for harm, anger, a no (or the missing yes), who's accountable and what's possible in practice, all that still gets its real name. So this was never about being positive whether it's true or not. It's about where the words go once the truth's been said, toward what you'd choose to protect or repair, and what can still be practiced or grown.

t69d_st5f: This can be borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form. The peer doesn't become your permanent parent (that's kind of the point). They show you something they can do and help you join in, and then they hand it back. Afterward, name what you got from them, and do one piece of it for yourself. Therapy is still useful for what therapy does. Community and disciplined peer support just do something different, and a serious healing path can include both.

# Speak Toward What You Are Building

Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: "Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, give you ideas, or some mix?" Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time. If it's obvious what they want, go with that. If it isn't, that one sentence can keep you from advising somebody who's thinking, "I just need you to hear this." Or from just listening while they're asking for help thinking.

The basic premise of [Hearthwork](https://hearthwork.u-dont-exist.com), my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time. Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing. You speak. I listen. Then we switch. Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality. It's kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.

Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time's up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don't push. But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places.

Community can work in both directions, too. Sometimes loving people give somebody enough safety and belonging that a deeper opening becomes possible. Other times it's the other way around. Somebody has a big opening first, a love or a meaning they couldn't have imagined before, and then they start to "manifest" different kinds of people and relationships in their life. Either way, the community is what helps make it practical, real, down to earth, embodied and so on.

This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with building community. Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn't really the point. The love has to move, and it doesn't always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop). From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into the grown-up relationship, then out to other people, and back again.
